title: TCP TIME_WAIT State, Ephemeral Port Ranges & Connection Reuse

spark.summary: The active closer of a TCP connection enters TIME_WAIT for 2*MSL (60s on Linux) to absorb delayed duplicate packets; opening unpooled outbound connections exhausts all 28,232 default ephemeral ports at just 470 req/s, failing with EADDRNOTAVAIL.
spark.keyTakeaway: TIME_WAIT is a deliberate RFC 9293 safety mechanism—fix port exhaustion by reusing sockets via HTTP Keep-Alive pooling, widening ip_local_port_range, and enabling tcp_tw_reuse=1 (never tcp_tw_recycle).
spark.byteSummary:
During TCP's 4-way teardown (`FIN -> ACK -> FIN -> ACK`), whichever side sends the final `ACK` (the active closer) enters `TIME_WAIT` for `2 * MSL` (hardcoded to 60 seconds in Linux). This guard prevents two hazards: ensuring the passive closer receives the final `ACK` if lost, and preventing delayed duplicate segments from a previous connection from corrupting a new connection on the same 4-tuple.

Because Linux defaults `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range` to `32768..60999` (only 28,232 ports), an API gateway making unpooled outbound HTTP calls to a single upstream `(dst_ip, dst_port)` saturates its entire port pool at just `28,232 / 60 = 470 req/s`, failing new `connect()` calls with `EADDRNOTAVAIL` while CPU sits idle.

Resolving `TIME_WAIT` storms relies on eliminating socket churn via persistent HTTP Keep-Alive / HTTP/2 connection pooling, widening `ip_local_port_range` to `1024..65535` (64,511 ports), enabling `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1` with TCP timestamps, and adding multi-IP SNAT diversity.

learningJourney.title: Stage 1: TCP 4-Way Teardown & Why TIME_WAIT Exists
learningJourney.purpose: Understand the two RFC 9293 guarantees provided by the 60-second 2*MSL TIME_WAIT state.
learningJourney.explanation: When a client or gateway closes a TCP socket first (active close), it sends `FIN`, receives `ACK`/`FIN`, and transmits the final `ACK`. It must remain in `TIME_WAIT` for `2 * MSL` (60s on Linux) so: (1) if the final `ACK` is dropped, it can retransmit it on `FIN` retry; and (2) stale in-flight packets expire before the same 4-tuple is reused.

sectionDiagram.title: Why the Active Closer Holds the 4-Tuple in 60s TIME_WAIT

cards.label: Active vs Passive Closer
cards.detail: Only the side that initiates close() first enters TIME_WAIT; servers letting clients close first avoid holding TIME_WAIT.

cards.label: 470 req/s Ceiling
cards.detail: 28,232 default ports / 60s = 470.5 new connections/sec per (src_ip, dst_ip, dst_port) tuple.

sectionDiagram.summary: The active closer holds TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds to retransmit lost final ACKs and drain delayed duplicate packets.
sectionDiagram.caption: TCP's active closer enters 60s TIME_WAIT after the final ACK to guard against lost ACKs and delayed duplicates.

learningJourney.title: Stage 2: The 4-Tuple & Linux Ephemeral Port Exhaustion
learningJourney.purpose: Explain why 28,232 ephemeral ports cap unpooled throughput per destination and trigger EADDRNOTAVAIL.
learningJourney.explanation: A TCP connection is uniquely identified by `(src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port)`. When an outbound client connects to a single upstream VIP `(dst_ip, dst_port)` from one `src_ip`, only `src_port` varies—drawing from `ip_local_port_range` (`32768..60999` = 28,232 ports). Once all 28,232 sit in `TIME_WAIT`, `connect()` fails with `EADDRNOTAVAIL`.

sectionDiagram.title: Saturating 28,232 Ephemeral Ports at 470+ Unpooled Req/Sec

cards.label: Low-CPU Failure Signature
cards.detail: Port exhaustion returns EADDRNOTAVAIL immediately without burning CPU, appearing as 502s at ~30% CPU.

cards.label: Conntrack Amplification
cards.detail: High TIME_WAIT churn can also fill nf_conntrack_max tables in Kubernetes/NAT nodes, dropping packets silently.

sectionDiagram.summary: With fixed destination IP/port and one source IP, 28,232 default ephemeral ports saturate at 470 unpooled req/s.
sectionDiagram.caption: Fixed (src_ip, dst_ip, dst_port) leaves only 28,232 src_ports, saturating in 60s TIME_WAIT at 470 req/s.

learningJourney.title: Stage 3: HTTP Keep-Alive & Persistent Connection Pooling
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate socket churn completely by reusing a small pool of persistent TCP/HTTP2 connections.
learningJourney.explanation: The primary fix for `TIME_WAIT` exhaustion is never closing sockets per request. Configuring HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive pools (e.g., 256 persistent connections) or multiplexed HTTP/2 / gRPC channels lets 40,000+ req/sec flow over 256 open sockets—dropping `TIME_WAIT` sockets from 28,232 to near zero while saving TLS/TCP handshake latency.

sectionDiagram.title: Serving 40,000 Req/Sec Over 256 Persistent Keep-Alive Sockets

cards.label: Set Client Idle < Server Idle
cards.detail: Configure client pool idle timeout (e.g., 55s) shorter than server keepalive_timeout (65s) to prevent race-condition EOFs.

cards.label: NGINX Upstream Trap
cards.detail: In NGINX, proxy_http_version 1.1 and proxy_set_header Connection "" are required or keepalive silently closes every socket!

sectionDiagram.summary: Persistent HTTP Keep-Alive pooling (256 sockets) serves 40,000+ req/sec with zero TIME_WAIT churn.
sectionDiagram.caption: 256 persistent Keep-Alive sockets serve 40,000+ req/sec without per-request TCP/TLS handshakes or TIME_WAIT buildup.

learningJourney.title: Stage 4: Kernel Tuning — ip_local_port_range & tcp_tw_reuse
learningJourney.purpose: Safely expand ephemeral port headroom and enable RFC 7323 timestamp-based TIME_WAIT reuse.
learningJourney.explanation: As a secondary defense for short-lived bursty clients, widen `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 1024 65535` (doubling capacity from 28,232 to 64,511 ports) and set `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1` (or `2` for loopback-only), which safely reuses `TIME_WAIT` sockets for outbound `connect()` when TCP timestamps (`tcp_timestamps = 1`) prove the new packet is newer.

sectionDiagram.title: Widening Ephemeral Ports & Timestamp-Safe tcp_tw_reuse

cards.label: Why tcp_tw_recycle Was Removed
cards.detail: tcp_tw_recycle broke behind NATs because clients share one IP with unsynchronized clocks, dropping legitimate SYNs.

cards.label: Listen-Port Collisions
cards.detail: Reserve specific server listen ports (e.g., 8080, 9090) via ip_local_reserved_ports so outbound sockets don't grab them.

sectionDiagram.summary: Widening ip_local_port_range to 1024..65535 and enabling tcp_tw_reuse=1 with timestamps adds safe outbound port headroom.
sectionDiagram.caption: ip_local_port_range=1024..65535 and tcp_tw_reuse=1 with tcp_timestamps=1 safely expand outbound port reuse.

learningJourney.title: Stage 5: Multi-IP SNAT Diversity & 4-Tuple Scaling
learningJourney.purpose: Scale past 64,511 sockets when connecting to a single upstream VIP using multiple source IPs or IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT.
learningJourney.explanation: If a proxy legitimately needs > 64,511 concurrent connections to one `(dst_ip, dst_port)` (e.g., 200K WebSockets), a single `src_ip` cannot exceed 64K ports. Assigning M source IPs (`SNAT` pool or `bind()` across M IPs with `IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT`) multiplies unique 4-tuples to `M * 64,511`.

sectionDiagram.title: Multiplying Port Capacity with Multi-IP SNAT & IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT

cards.label: IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT
cards.detail: Calling bind(src_ip, port=0) without this flag locks the port globally across all destinations instead of per-destination 4-tuple!

cards.label: Conntrack Sizing
cards.detail: Scale nf_conntrack_max proportionally when running multi-IP SNAT gateways.

sectionDiagram.summary: Multi-IP SNAT pools paired with IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT multiply outbound 4-tuple capacity to M * 64,511 sockets.
sectionDiagram.caption: Multi-IP SNAT pools and IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT multiply unique 4-tuples beyond the 64,511 single-IP ceiling.

learningJourney.title: Stage 6: Avoiding SO_LINGER RST Anti-Patterns
learningJourney.purpose: Explain why setting SO_LINGER(on, 0) to skip TIME_WAIT causes silent data corruption and connection resets.
learningJourney.explanation: Some developers try to bypass `TIME_WAIT` by setting `SO_LINGER` with `l_linger = 0`, forcing the kernel to send `RST` instead of `FIN`. That aborts unread buffered data on the peer, throws `ECONNRESET` in clients, and removes the `2*MSL` duplicate-packet shield—corrupting subsequent connections on that port.

sectionDiagram.title: Why SO_LINGER(0) RST Bypasses Corrupt In-Flight Streams

cards.label: Silent Payload Truncation
cards.detail: An immediate RST can wipe unread tail bytes in the peer's TCP receive buffer even after send() succeeded locally.

cards.label: Valid RST Use Case
cards.detail: Only use RST when intentionally aborting a half-open or protocol-violating malicious connection.

sectionDiagram.summary: Never use SO_LINGER(0) RST to bypass TIME_WAIT; it causes ECONNRESET failures and loses the 2*MSL duplicate-packet shield.
sectionDiagram.caption: SO_LINGER(0) RST shortcuts trigger ECONNRESET and strip 2*MSL protection; use Keep-Alive and tcp_tw_reuse instead.

learningJourney.title: Stage 7: Live Socket Telemetry & Ephemeral Port Alerting
learningJourney.purpose: Detect TIME_WAIT buildup early using ss -s, conntrack metrics, and port-utilization SLO alerts.
learningJourney.explanation: Export `node_sockstat_TCP_tw` and `node_netstat_TcpExt_TCPTimeWaitOverflow` from Prometheus `node_exporter`, alongside `ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l` and `nf_conntrack_count / nf_conntrack_max`. Alert at 60% ephemeral port utilization so teams fix Keep-Alive misconfigurations before `EADDRNOTAVAIL` 502s occur.

sectionDiagram.title: Monitoring TCP_tw, Conntrack & Pool Hit Rates Before 502s

cards.label: New-Conn/Sec Ratio
cards.detail: If new outbound TCP connects/sec exceeds 1% of total RPS on an HTTP gateway, Keep-Alive pooling is broken.

cards.label: Per-Container Namespace
cards.detail: Remember Kubernetes pods have isolated network namespaces—check ip_local_port_range inside the pod netns, not just the host.

sectionDiagram.summary: Monitoring TCP_tw ratio, conntrack utilization, and new-connections/sec catches broken Keep-Alive pools before 502s hit.
sectionDiagram.caption: Monitoring TCP_tw, conntrack usage, and gateway new-connections/sec alerts on port exhaustion before 502s occur.

knowledgeChecks.question: With Linux's default `ip_local_port_range` (32768..60999 = 28,232 ports) and 60s `TIME_WAIT`, what is the maximum unpooled outbound RPS to a single `(dst_ip, dst_port)`?

options.feedback: Correct. Once 470 req/s sustain for 60s, all 28,232 ports sit in TIME_WAIT and new connect() calls fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL.
Incorrect. 65,535 is total 16-bit port space, and 60s TIME_WAIT divides the usable range by 60.
Incorrect. That ignores the 60-second TIME_WAIT hold duration.

options.text: Unlimited req/s as long as CPU < 50%.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Port exhaustion happens independently of CPU utilization.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: 28,232 ephemeral ports divided by 60 seconds yields a hard ceiling of ~470 unpooled connections/sec per target tuple.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why did Linux 4.12 remove `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_recycle` while keeping `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse`?

options.text: `tcp_tw_recycle` broke connections behind shared-IP NATs due to differing client timestamps, whereas `tcp_tw_reuse` safely applies only to outbound `connect()` with PAWS.
options.feedback: Correct. Multiple clients behind a NAT have different clocks, causing tcp_tw_recycle to drop legitimate SYN packets.

options.text: `tcp_tw_recycle` forced every socket to stay open for 10 minutes.
options.feedback: Incorrect. It aggressively recycled TIME_WAIT based on per-IP timestamps, breaking NAT traffic.
Incorrect. tcp_tw_reuse works alongside Keep-Alive for outbound sockets.
Incorrect. It failed on IPv4 NATs.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: tcp_tw_recycle dropped legitimate SYNs from NATed clients with skewed timestamps; tcp_tw_reuse=1 is safe for outbound connections.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should you NEVER set `SO_LINGER(on, 0)` to send `RST` and skip `TIME_WAIT`?

options.text: Sending `RST` aborts unread data in the peer's receive buffer (`ECONNRESET`) and strips the 2*MSL shield against delayed duplicate packets.
options.feedback: Correct. Skipping FIN/TIME_WAIT risks silent truncation and packet corruption on reused ports.
Incorrect. It skips TIME_WAIT via RST, which is unsafe.
Incorrect. It is a socket close option, unrelated to HTTP/2.

options.text: Because Linux only allows `SO_LINGER` on UDP sockets.
options.feedback: Incorrect. SO_LINGER is a TCP socket option.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Using SO_LINGER(0) sends RST instead of FIN, causing ECONNRESET on peers and exposing reused 4-tuples to stale packets.

beginner.summary: Closing a TCP connection locks its port for 60 seconds (`TIME_WAIT`); reusing connections via HTTP Keep-Alive prevents running out of ports.
beginner.keyTakeaway: Persistent Keep-Alive connection pools let thousands of requests share a few hundred sockets without hitting `EADDRNOTAVAIL`.
beginner.byteSummary:
When a server opens and closes a new TCP connection for every request, Linux holds each port for 60 seconds in `TIME_WAIT`. At just 470 requests/sec, all 28,232 default ports get used up.

Using HTTP Keep-Alive connection pooling reuses a small set of open connections so ports never run out.

intermediate.summary: Eliminate `EADDRNOTAVAIL` at 40K+ req/s by enabling 256-socket HTTP Keep-Alive pooling, widening `ip_local_port_range` to `1024..65535`, and setting `tcp_tw_reuse=1`.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: Fix NGINX/Envoy Keep-Alive headers (`proxy_http_version 1.1`), widen ephemeral ports to 64,511, and never use `tcp_tw_recycle`.
intermediate.byteSummary:
In Production Scenario #29, 40,000 outbound req/s hit 35% `EADDRNOTAVAIL` failures at 30% CPU because unpooled sockets pinned all 28,232 ports in 60s `TIME_WAIT`.

Enabling a 256-socket Keep-Alive pool, widening `ip_local_port_range` to `1024..65535`, and setting `tcp_tw_reuse=1` eliminates port exhaustion.

advanced.summary: Scale beyond 64K concurrent sockets with multi-IP SNAT + `IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT`, avoid `SO_LINGER(0)` RST corruption, and alert on `TCP_tw` + conntrack.
advanced.keyTakeaway: Pair `IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT` with multi-IP SNAT for >64K sockets and monitor `node_sockstat_TCP_tw` inside pod netns.
advanced.byteSummary:
To scale past the 64,511 single-IP port cap, use multi-IP SNAT pools with `IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT` (avoiding global port-0 bind locks) and avoid `SO_LINGER(0)` RST shortcuts.

Monitor `node_sockstat_TCP_tw`, `nf_conntrack` utilization, and gateway new-connections/sec inside Kubernetes pod network namespaces.
